title: Public Space Use By-law approved with encampment funding
subtitle: Square protections added, $450,000 for basic needs, portable washroom and sharps plan, long delegation hearing, legal and accessibility concerns
overview: Council met in a special meeting to consider a Public Space Use By-law governing temporary shelters and tents on city property. After a closed session on legal advice, where the mayor reported council only received information, the open meeting heard staff, police and county representatives, then dozens of delegates. Council approved the by-law {{vote:m5}}, after amending it to treat all of St. George's Square and Market Square as sensitive public areas {{vote:m4}}. It returns for final adoption on September 10 and would take effect October 1.

Staff said the by-law is not meant to ban encampments. Many parks and vacant lands would be permitted at all times, sports fields and squares would allow overnight shelters only, and sensitive or designated areas would not allow them. Staff are not recommending fines, and plan education, outreach and a public map.

Council also committed up to $450,000 from a reserve for basic needs for people experiencing homelessness, delivered through the county and the Health and Housing Community Planning Table {{vote:m6}}. Staff will also develop a plan and budget for portable washrooms, waste bins and sharps disposal at encampments, reporting back in early 2025 {{vote:m7}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved the draft by-law as amended and directed staff to bring it to the September 10, 2024 meeting for final adoption, taking effect October 1, 2024 {{vote:m5}}.
Staff will amend Schedule A so all of St. George's Square and Market Square are sensitive public areas {{vote:m4}}.

Up to $450,000 one-time funding from the Tax Rate Operating Contingency Reserve goes to the County of Wellington for basic needs through the planning table, from September 2024 to December 2025, reduced if senior-government funds are found {{vote:m6}}.

Staff will work with the planning table on a plan, budget and funding source for portable washrooms, waste bins and sharps disposal at encampments, subject to site feasibility, reporting in Q1 2025 {{vote:m7}}.

debate: Supporters, including downtown business owners and residents near the river parks, described open drug use, garbage, fires, harassment and lost customers, and said rules are needed on where tents can be placed. Several said the by-law is imperfect but a step.

Opponents, including health, legal and community delegates, argued the by-law criminalizes homelessness, moves people away from services, and lacks consultation. A legal delegate said similar by-laws have been struck down elsewhere and that court action against the city was likely.

The chair of the Accessibility Advisory Committee said staff had committed to engage the committee before the by-law returned, which did not happen. Staff said work was paused after the Kingston appeal was withdrawn and planned to meet the committee in October.

Delegates and county staff described service gaps: no daytime drop-in hours in the morning, limited shelter capacity and growing demand. Some delegates urged tiny homes, dedicated sites or treatment-focused strategies instead.

Among councillors, supporters said the by-law resolves conflicts over bookable and sensitive spaces and is not a solution to homelessness. Opponents said it would not change much and would cost the city more than it solves.
